items: Except copper, which is reddish brown, they are silvery or grey lustrous metals.
Their atomic radius usually decreases from left to right but increases a little at the end; the increase at copper is linked to its completely filled d subshell.
They have high melting and boiling points, which vary irregularly across the row (Figure 18.1).
They are good conductors of electricity and heat.
They have high densities, which generally increase from titanium to copper as the nuclear charge builds up and the atoms shrink.
They are shiny, malleable (can be hammered into thin sheets) and ductile (can be drawn into wires).
Most of them and their compounds are paramagnetic (attracted by a magnet) because they have unpaired d electrons.

blocks.alt: Two line charts for Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni and Cu. Left: atomic radius falls from 147 pm (Ti) to 124 pm (Ni) and rises to 128 pm (Cu); ionic radius falls from 86 to 69 pm with Cu at 73. Right: boiling points 3287, 3407, 2672, 2061, 2862, 2870, 2913 and 2562 C; melting points 1688, 1910, 1907, 1246, 1538, 1495, 1455 and 1085 C.
blocks.caption: Atomic and ionic radii and melting and boiling points of the 3d elements (original charts after Figure 18.1).
blocks.long_description: Across the first row the atomic radius falls at first, because each step adds a proton to the nucleus while the extra electron goes into an inner 3d orbital that shields the outer 4s electrons poorly; from chromium to nickel the radius hardly changes, and copper is a little larger. The melting and boiling points are high because both 3d and 4s electrons take part in metallic bonding; they do not change smoothly, and manganese has unusually low values.

blocks.prompt: Which first-row transition metal has the lowest melting point in Figure 18.1?
blocks.explanation: Copper (1085 C); among Ti to Ni, manganese is unusually low (1246 C).

items: Hard, dense, lustrous, malleable and ductile; good conductors.
High melting and boiling points; many are paramagnetic.
